related-article.article-title: Comment on “Concomitant use of metformin and proton pump inhibitors increases vitamin B12 deficiency risk in type 2 diabetes”
Author's reply to the “Comment on ‘Concomitant use of metformin and proton pump inhibitors increases vitamin B12 deficiency risk in type 2 diabetes’”

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Vitamin B12 deficiency is one of the adverse drug reactions of metformin and proton pump inhibitors (PPIs). As symptoms of gastroesophageal reflux disease are frequently reported in patients with diabetes, the concomitant use of metformin and PPI is expected. Therefore, this study aimed to investigate the effects of concurrent PPI use on the risk of vitamin B12 deficiency in patients with type 2 diabetes (T2DM) using metformin.

sec.title: Materials and Methods
sec.p: This retrospective cohort study was conducted using a sample cohort database provided by the National Health Insurance Service. Among adult patients newly diagnosed with T2DM, new users of metformin who used metformin ≥4 months were included. The subjects were divided into two cohorts: metformin monotherapy and metformin + PPI. Vitamin B12 deficiency was defined by a diagnostic code or a prescription of medications for vitamin B12 supplementation. A Cox proportional hazards model was used to estimate the adjusted hazard ratio (aHR) with a 95% confidence interval (CI).

sec.title: Results
sec.p: In total, 11,200 subjects were included in the 1:1 propensity score‐matched cohort. The risk of vitamin B12 deficiency was significantly higher in the metformin + PPI cohort compared with the metformin monotherapy cohort (aHR, 1.18; 95% CI, 1.02–1.35).

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: A significant association between the concurrent use of metformin and PPI and an increased risk of vitamin B12 deficiency was found, highlighting the need to carefully monitor the symptoms associated with vitamin B12 deficiency and regularly assess vitamin B12 levels when considering the concomitant use of PPI and metformin.

abstract.p: The concomitant use of metformin and PPI was significantly associated with an increased risk of vitamin B12 deficiency in patients with type 2 diabetes.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: The prevalence of type 2 diabetes (T2DM) is increasing worldwide owing to an increase in the number of patients with obesity, a sedentary lifestyle, and unhealthy eating habits 1 . According to the International Diabetes Federation, the prevalence of T2DM in adults was approximately 10.5% in 2021, and it is expected to increase to 12.2% in 2045 2 . Metformin is an oral hypoglycemic agent that is commonly used as monotherapy or in combination with other hypoglycemic agents in patients with T2DM.

While metformin is generally safe for most people, reduced vitamin B12 status is known as a potential long‐term ADR of metformin use 3 . It is believed that metformin can induce vitamin B12 deficiency by inhibiting its calcium‐dependent receptor‐mediated absorption in the terminal ileum 4 . The reported prevalence of vitamin B12 deficiency according to metformin use varies depending on the duration of metformin use and the definition of vitamin B12 deficiency, but it ranges from 5.8% to 52% worldwide. In particular, a longer duration of metformin use is associated with a higher risk of developing vitamin B12 deficiency 5 .

It is crucial to manage vitamin B12 deficiency since untreated deficiency could lead to neurological or hematological clinical consequences beyond a simple decrease in blood vitamin B12 levels. While the mechanism how vitamin B12 deficiency leads to demyelination and related neurotoxicity remains unclear, several hypotheses have been suggested. As a coenzyme for homocysteine methyltransferase, vitamin B12 deficiency may cause a reduction in methionine and S‐adenosyl methionine 6 . This may induce demyelination of neurons, resulting in neurological abnormalities, such as neuropathy and motor loss. Other hypotheses explain that vitamin B12 deficiency has a proinflammatory effect, which could lead to the development of neuropathy 7 . Additionally, as vitamin B12 functions as a coenzyme for methionine synthase, low levels of it may hinder the synthesis of deoxyribonucleic acid in red blood cells, leading to megaloblastic anemia 8 .

Meanwhile, proton pump inhibitor (PPI), a treatment option for gastric acid‐related diseases such as gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and peptic ulcer disease, is also known as a risk factor for reduced vitamin B12 status. PPIs reduce gastric acid production, which is required for vitamin B12 to be released from dietary proteins, leading to malabsorption and deficiency in vitamin B12 9 . PPIs are particularly noteworthy for use in patients with diabetes because approximately 40% of these patients are reported to experience symptoms of GERD, and the risk of developing GERD in patients with diabetes is 1.6 times higher than that in patients without diabetes 10 , 11 .

Following a study published in 1994 that confirmed a significant reduction in vitamin B12 absorption when omeprazole was used for 2 weeks in a healthy study group, studies have continued to evaluate the association between PPI use and vitamin B12 deficiency 12 . For instance, one study found that the use of PPI for more than 2 years was associated with a significant increase in the risk of vitamin B12 deficiency 13 . Moreover, a recent systematic review of seven related studies concluded that the long‐term use of PPI may affect vitamin B12 absorption 14 .

While numerous studies have examined the association between vitamin B12 deficiency with each drug individually, only a few have assessed the combined effect of concurrent metformin and PPIs use on vitamin B12 deficiency in patients with T2D. Previous studies also have limitations, such as using a cross‐sectional design without accounting for confounders or having a limited sample size 15 , 16 . Thus, we aimed to evaluate the association between the concurrent use of metformin and PPIs and the risk of vitamin B12 deficiency, compared to using metformin alone, in adult patients with T2DM using a nationwide large‐scale database.

sec.title: Data source
sec.p: This study was conducted using the National Health Insurance Service‐National Sample Cohort (NHIS‐NSC), which is a stratified sampling of 2% of the entire Korean population and includes information on the medical use and socioeconomic status of approximately one million people from 2002 to 2019. The sample cohort consists of six tables: qualification and insurance eligibility, birth and death, treatment, medical check‐up, medical care institution, and long‐term care tables 11 .

The study protocol was reviewed and approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of Sookmyung Women's University (SMWU) (IRB number: SMWU‐2204‐HR‐016). The requirement for informed consent was waived because all data were anonymous.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: In this retrospective cohort study, the cohort entry date, or index date, was defined as the date on which metformin was first prescribed or the date on which metformin and PPI were concurrently initiated (Figure S1). Baseline characteristics, including age, sex, and income level, were investigated on the index date, and the period up to 1 year prior to the index date was set as the washout period to confirm whether PPI had been used and whether vitamin B12 deficiency had occurred. In addition, underlying diseases, drugs used during the same period, and drugs used during the follow‐up of study subjects were also evaluated as confounding variables.

sec.title: Study population
sec.p: This study included adult patients who were first diagnosed with T2DM from 2003 to 2019 and those who started using metformin for at least 4 months. These selection criteria were based on the results of a previous randomized controlled trial in which vitamin B12 levels were reduced from 4 months in patients with T2DM who started using metformin 12 . Patients with T2DM were defined as those who met the Korean Standard Classification of Diseases (KCD; E11–E14) and were prescribed at least one hypoglycemic agent during the study period.

To include patients diagnosed with T2DM for the first time during the study period only, those diagnosed with T2DM in 2002 were excluded from this study. Additionally, patients who were not adults at the time of the cohort entry date and those whose cohort entry date matched the vitamin B12 deficiency onset date, death date, or study end date (December 31, 2019) were excluded. Patients with a history of PPI use or vitamin B12 deficiency, when evaluated 1 year prior to the cohort entry date, were also excluded from this study. The following eight PPIs were included in this study: omeprazole, esomeprazole, lansoprazole, dexlansoprazole, pantoprazole, S‐pantoprazole, rabeprazole, and ilaprazole.

sec.title: Drug exposure assessment
sec.p: In this study, exposure to metformin or PPI was assessed using an intention‐to‐treat approach. It was assumed that the drug used for the first time was used until the end of the follow‐up period, regardless of drug discontinuation or replacement. Accordingly, each study subject was followed up to the earliest event among the date of occurrence of vitamin B12 deficiency, death, and the end of this study.

The duration of continued medication use was defined as the grace period. It was assumed that the drug was continuously used if the start date of treatment for the next prescription was before the date obtained by adding 1.5 times the total administration days to the end date of treatment for the previous prescription.

The concomitant use of metformin and PPI was defined as a case in which PPI use lasted for at least 2 weeks and overlapped with continuous use of metformin. This definition was based on a previous study that reported a significant decrease in vitamin B12 absorption after at least 2 weeks of PPI use 6 .

sec.title: Outcome
sec.p: The outcome variable of this study was vitamin B12 deficiency. Vitamin B12 deficiency was defined as having a related KCD code or being prescribed a medication for vitamin B12 supplementation. The disease codes included E538 (deficiency of other specified B group vitamins, including vitamin B12), D51 (vitamin B12 deficiency anemia), and G320 (subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord in vitamin B12 deficiency). For these drugs, a single agent of mecobalamin, hydroxocobalamin, and cobamamide was considered.

sec.title: Covariates
sec.p: In this study, covariates that may affect the risk of vitamin B12 deficiency following the concurrent use of metformin and PPI were considered. Demographic and sociological variables, including age, sex, and income level, were evaluated at the time of cohort enrollment. Income levels were divided into three groups based on insurance premiums. The Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) score was calculated using the comorbidities evaluated up to 1 year prior to the cohort enrollment date and then categorized into five groups. Other underlying diseases, including hypertension, dyslipidemia, cancer, and GERD, were also evaluated up to 1 year prior to the date of cohort enrollment.

Comorbidities and drug use, which are known as risk factors for vitamin B12 deficiency, were considered confounding variables. The evaluation period for comorbidities was 1 year before the index date, and the comorbidities included intestinal malabsorption, postprocedural disorders of the digestive system, chronic atrophic gastritis, inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis), and exocrine pancreatic insufficiency. H2 receptor antagonist (H2RA), nitrous oxide, and colchicine were considered, and the use of these drugs was investigated up to 1 year before the cohort enrollment date and during the follow‐up period.

sec.title: Statistical analyses
sec.p: Propensity score (PS) matching was conducted after applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria to the study population. PS was estimated using a multivariate logistic regression model, in which age, sex, income level, CCI score, comorbidities, and drug use as risk factors for vitamin B12 deficiency were included as covariates. Based on the calculated PS, the metformin monotherapy and metformin + PPI groups were matched at a 1:1 ratio, which had the highest number of total patients.

For the baseline characteristics of the patients included in the pre‐ and post‐matching cohorts, continuous variables were presented as means and standard deviations, and categorical variables were presented as frequencies and percentages. In addition, standardized differences (SDs) were estimated to evaluate the potential imbalance of covariates before and after matching, with a value <0.1 indicating a significant balance.

After PS matching, along with the incidence rate (IR) within each group, incidence rate ratio (IRR) and hazard ratio (HR) using a Cox proportional hazards model were used to evaluate the risk of vitamin B12 deficiency according to the concomitant use of PPI and metformin. HR and 95% confidence interval (CI) were estimated according to the following three models: model 1, unadjusted; model 2, co‐medications during the follow‐up; and model 3, co‐medications during the follow‐up, age, income level, CCI score, comorbidities, and medication use in the year prior to the index date.

Subgroup analyses based on age and sex were performed to evaluate whether the association between the concomitant use of medications and the occurrence of vitamin B12 deficiency changes according to the population characteristics. In addition, sensitivity analysis was performed using the as‐treated method rather than the intention‐to‐treat method to determine whether the main study results differ depending on the definition of drug exposure. In this case, each study subject was followed up until the earliest event among the onset of vitamin B12 deficiency, discontinuation of the drug, death, and end of this study.
All statistical analyses were performed using SAS Enterprise Guide version 7.13, and a P‐value <0.05 was considered statistically significant.

sec.title: RESULTS
sec.p: Of the 117,727 patients who were newly diagnosed with T2DM between 2003 and 2019, 53,115 patients used metformin for ≥4 months. After applying the exclusion criteria, 42,152 patients were included in this study. Finally, after 1:1 PS matching, a total of 11,200 patients were included in this study (Figure 1). After PS matching, the SD of all variables, including age, sex, income level, CCI score, comorbidity, and history of drug use, was <0.1, indicating that the baseline characteristics were well balanced between the metformin monotherapy group and metformin + PPI group (Table 1).

sec.p: During the follow‐up period, vitamin B12 deficiency was observed in 8.3% (n = 464) patients in the metformin monotherapy cohort and 7.2% (n = 403) patients in the metformin + PPI cohort. The total person‐years were 32,345.0 and 26,143.8 years in the metformin monotherapy and metformin + PPI cohorts, respectively. In the Cox proportional hazards model 1, the concurrent use of metformin and PPI did not significantly increase the risk of vitamin B12 deficiency (adjusted HR [aHR], 1.08; 95% CI, 0.94–1.24). However, when co‐medications during the follow‐up, age, income level, CCI score, comorbidities, and medication use in the year prior to the index date were adjusted, the concomitant use of PPI was associated with an 18% higher risk of vitamin B12 deficiency compared with metformin monotherapy (aHR, 1.18; 95% CI, 1.02–1.35; Table 2).

sec.p: Among the 11,200 patients included in the 1:1 PS‐matched cohort, 7,014 were aged <65 years, and 4,186 were aged ≥65 years. The IRR of vitamin B12 deficiency in the concomitant metformin and PPI group, relative to the metformin‐only group, was higher in patients aged ≥65 years (1.12) than in patients aged <65 years (1.04). In the full‐adjusted model 3, concurrent PPI use was associated with a higher risk of vitamin B12 deficiency compared with metformin monotherapy in both age groups, consistent with the pooled result. However, the association was not statistically significant (aHR, 1.20; 95% CI, 0.99–1.46 in <65 years; aHR, 1.16; 95% CI, 0.94–1.43 in ≥65 years). Similarly, in the subgroup analysis by sex, increased risk of vitamin B12 deficiency was observed in both males (n = 5,999) and females (n = 5,201) in the full‐adjusted model 3, but no statistical significance was found (aHR, 1.16; 95% CI, 0.95–1.42 in males; aHR, 1.20; 95% CI, 0.99–1.47 in females; Table 3).

sec.p: A sensitivity analysis was performed using the as‐treated approach for drug exposure evaluation. As a result, 170 and 30 cases of vitamin B12 deficiency were observed in the metformin monotherapy and the metformin + PPI groups, respectively, and the total person‐years were 14,799.8 and 1,589.8 years, respectively. In the full‐adjusted Cox proportional hazards model 3, the concurrent use of metformin and PPI significantly increased the risk of vitamin B12 deficiency (aHR, 1.78; 95% CI, 1.15–2.75), which was consistent with the main findings (aHR, 1.18; 95% CI, 1.02–1.35; Table S1 and Figure S2).

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: This retrospective cohort study aimed to investigate the effects of concurrent PPI use on vitamin B12 deficiency in patients with T2DM using metformin with the sample cohort database of the NHIS. In the 1:1 PS‐matched cohort, the association between concomitant use of PPI and metformin and the risk of vitamin B12 deficiency was evaluated using the Cox proportional hazards model. A subgroup analysis stratified by age (65 years) and sex was also performed. Compared with metformin alone, the combined use of metformin and PPI was associated with a significantly higher risk of vitamin B12 deficiency. However, in the subgroup analysis, no significant increase in the risk of developing vitamin B12 deficiency was observed with concurrent use of metformin and PPI in any subgroup.

In this study, among the patients with T2DM who used metformin for ≥4 months, those who used metformin and PPI concomitantly had a higher risk of vitamin B12 deficiency by 18% compared with those treated with metformin monotherapy. A sensitivity analysis, where drug exposure was evaluated using an as‐treated approach instead of an intention‐to‐treat approach, showed consistent results with the primary analysis. This result corroborates that of a previous study that reported that among patients with T2D who have taken metformin over 1 year, PPI use was associated with 3–8 times higher risk of developing vitamin deficiency, defined as serum vitamin <179.3 pg/mL, compared to those who have not used PPI 17 . Another cross‐section study reported that concomitant use of a PPI or H2RA was significantly associated with an increased risk of vitamin B12 deficiency (≤200 pg/mL) in patients who had been using metformin for ≥3 months (adjusted odds ratio, 1.79; 95% CI, 1.47–2.18) 13 . Similarly, a retrospective study reported that the incidence of vitamin B12 deficiency (<300 pg/mL) was significantly higher among those who used concomitant PPI and metformin (34.2%) compared to that in metformin‐only (22.2%) and PPI‐only (25.6%) groups 14 .

However, some studies have reported contradictory results. In a study conducted on patients who used metformin for ≥3 months in a diabetes center, no significant association was found between the concurrent use of PPI or H2RA and an increased risk of vitamin B12 deficiency (≤300 pg/mL) 15 . In addition, when the risk of vitamin B12 deficiency (≤298.1 pg/mL or ≤203.3 pg/mL) was evaluated according to the concomitant use of PPI or H2RA in patients with diabetes using metformin in Hong Kong, a significant association was not found 16 .

These mixed results are believed to be due to differences in the definitions of vitamin B12 deficiency applied to each study and the duration of metformin use by the study subjects. With regard to the serum vitamin B12 level, <200 pg/mL is defined as “deficiency,” and 200–300 pg/mL is defined as “borderline” or “insufficient,” generally, and different reference values are applied for each study 17 . In addition, when defining vitamin B12 deficiency, using blood vitamin B12 concentration with other biomarkers, such as methylmalonic acid (MMA), holotranscobalamin, and homocysteine, can explain vitamin B12 deficiency more accurately 18 . Therefore, a study using a more consistent and accurate definition of vitamin B12 deficiency is required to identify a clear association between the combination of metformin and PPI use and the occurrence of vitamin B12 deficiency.

In this study, we evaluated whether the association between the risk of vitamin B12 deficiency and concurrent use of metformin and PPI appears differently according to the age group. As a result, compared with using metformin alone, the concomitant use of PPI and metformin was associated with a higher risk of vitamin B12 deficiency in both age groups. However, a definitive comparison of the effect size between the age groups cannot be made, as the association was not statistically significant.

Besides, we found that the IRR of the outcome in the concomitant metformin and PPI group, compared to metformin‐only group, was greater in the patients aged ≥65 years (1.12) than in patients aged <65 years (1.04). This can be interpreted to mean that the relative risk of vitamin B12 deficiency according to the combination use of metformin and PPI may be more prominent in elderly patients than in younger patients. In general, the elderly are evaluated as a group of patients who are at risk of vitamin B12 deficiency due to reduced gastric acid secretion and excessive proliferation of intestinal bacteria owing to a decrease in physical function 19 . Therefore, when starting PPI concomitantly in elderly patients using metformin, vitamin B12 levels and deficiency‐related symptoms should be carefully monitored, considering the elderly's baseline characteristics.

In a subgroup analysis by sex, although not statistically significant, the concurrent use of PPI and metformin was associated with an increased risk of developing vitamin B12 deficiency in both males and females. IRR value was also comparable between men (1.07) and women (1.08). Further studies are needed to examine whether sex influences the association between the concurrent use of metformin and PPI and the risk of vitamin B12 deficiency.

A key strength of this study is the use of the sample cohort database of the NHIS, which enabled long‐term follow‐up in a large, representative population. By accounting for various potential confounders, including comorbidities and concomitant medications, the analysis provides a robust assessment of the association between concurrent use of metformin and PPI and vitamin B12 deficiency. Another strength is this study reflects clinically recognized deficiency rather than subclinical or biochemical changes alone, making the results more applicable to real‐world clinical practice. In addition, this study is meaningful as it evaluates the risk of vitamin B12 deficiency associated with specific drug combinations in patients with T2DM, a population with a high risk of ADRs due to the use of multiple drugs. Our findings underscore the importance of understanding the impact of commonly used medications in this group, which is clinically relevant for optimizing patient care and minimizing potential complications.

However, this study has some limitations. Due to the inherent constraints of using a secondary database, we used disease codes and prescription records to define the occurrence of vitamin B12 deficiency. This method may introduce misclassification bias, as some cases of vitamin B12 deficiency might not have been captured, while others may have been inaccurately classified. Moreover, now that vitamin B12 supplements are prescribed both for treatment and prophylaxis, prescription records to define the outcome may have resulted in the inclusion of patients who were not truly deficient but were at risk of developing deficiency. However, we attempted to mitigate this issue by adjusting for baseline comorbidities known to increase the risk of vitamin B12 deficiency, such as intestinal malabsorption and postprocedural disorders of the digestive system.

Additionally, the study results may have been underestimated because the intention‐to‐treat approach accounts for patients until the end of follow‐up regardless of drug discontinuation, thereby increasing total person‐years. However, we observed a consistent result from a sensitivity analysis based on an as‐treated approach, which further confirmed the association between the concomitant use of metformin and PPI and an increased risk of vitamin B12 deficiency compared with metformin monotherapy. Finally, due to the inherent limitations of the insurance claims data, the potential influence of unmeasured confounding variables, such as serum vitamin B12 levels and dietary factors, cannot be completely ruled out. For example, the risk of vitamin B12 deficiency may have decreased due to the intake of nutritional supplements, such as multivitamins, and may have increased due to a vegan diet. It is necessary to prospectively evaluate the effect of the concurrent use of metformin and PPI on vitamin B12 deficiency through further studies that consider all relevant confounding variables.

In conclusion, a significant association was confirmed between the concurrent use of PPI and the increased risk of vitamin B12 deficiency in adult patients with T2DM using metformin in this study. In particular, if metformin is taken for ≥4 months and a PPI is used in combination for ≥2 weeks, careful monitoring of symptoms related to vitamin B12 deficiency and regular assessment of vitamin B12 levels are required. This study serves as the basis for a follow‐up study that prospectively investigates the risk of ADRs induced by the concomitant use of drugs in patients with T2DM.

sec.title: DISCLOSURE
sec.p: The authors declare no conflict of interest.

Approval of the research protocol: The study protocol was reviewed and approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of Sookmyung Women's University (SMWU; IRB number: SMWU‐2204‐HR‐016). The requirement for informed consent was waived because all data were anonymous.
Informed consent: N/A.

Approval date of registry and the registration no. of the study/trial: This study utilized secondary data sources, specifically the National Health Insurance Service‐National Sample Cohort (NHIS‐NSC). As the research involved analysis of publicly available data and did not include direct interaction with human subjects, ethical approval was not required. Consequently, there is no applicable approval date or registration number for this study.
Animal studies: N/A.
